summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law permits only the issue of a new birth certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. Visitors carrying both records, or documents issued at different times, should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

On 10 December 2015 the States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting; the States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Discrimination protections were built up in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, by 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a twelve-month deferral from around 7 November 2011, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era. Other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Custodial safeguards are undocumented. Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.
tangentialFactors:
Guernsey sits outside the United Kingdom's statutory equality framework, so protections that trans visitors might assume from United Kingdom law are absent unless the States have legislated locally. The absence of any local equivalent to the 2025 single-sex-services code means bathroom and facility access in Guernsey is governed by practice and by the island's own anti-discrimination regime rather than by a codified national rule.

Jersey, the neighbouring Channel Island, approved the same removal of the bar on unmarried couples adopting two days before Guernsey did on 24 June 2015, indicating a shared regional direction on family recognition rather than an isolated local reform.

Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil-partnership legislation of its own, though United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012. Couples therefore hold marriage rights locally but must rely on recognition of an externally created status for succession.

The residual male homosexual offences are the main divergence from neighbouring practice: conduct lawful elsewhere can still attract prosecution in Guernsey if not conducted in private. That is a live exposure rather than a dormant provision on the statute book.

The September 2022 anti-discrimination bill passed the States of Guernsey unanimously, 33 votes to 0, and the house rejected proposed exemptions for businesses with five employees or fewer and for religiously affiliated organisations, so the protection reaches small employers and faith bodies alike.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory states how Les Nicolles assigns trans prisoners to wings by birth sex or gender identity, whether any protective placement or segregation practice exists, or how a trans detainee would be searched. The absence of a recorded rule is unresolved, not a finding that no practice exists.

Nothing sourced addresses hate-crime charging, police recording of anti-trans incidents, or violence against trans people in Guernsey; the anti-discrimination statute's enforcement record since 1 October 2023 is likewise not covered by the available material.

The inventory contains no entry, visa, border-screening or customs information for Guernsey, and no data on whether travel documents are examined for gender markers on arrival.

Local policy on single-sex facilities, including public lavatories, changing rooms and hospital wards, is not sourced. The non-application of the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex-services code is established, but what replaces it in Guernsey practice is unresolved.

Whether the retained male homosexual offences have been charged in recent decades, and whether any review of them is before the States, is not stated in the sources.
